5134.dq: Such syllables do not occur on the final edge of a word and may be derived through shortening of syllables in weak prosodic positions; in these iambic languages that is the initial edge of a prosodic foot.
5134.prule: Tone language, no stress rule. Lawngtlang Zophei is analysed with an underlying H vs. L vs. toneless contrast on every syllable (surface L, M, H and falling HM/ML, plus derived rises). Word prosody is described structurally as iambic sesquisyllables: one or more reduced 'minor' syllables (Ca, [ə], shorter, reduced contrasts) sit in the weak position, the initial edge of the prosodic foot, and the full 'major' syllable is the prominent one; minor syllables never occur at the final edge of a word/prosodic phrase, so the prominent major syllable is final in a sesquisyllable. No 'stress falls on syllable X' statement and no contrastive stress is claimed for Zophei.
5134.quote: [p.141] Minor syllables (or semi-, reduced, or pre-syllables) are similar to the Vʔ rhymes discussed above in that they are shorter and often offer fewer contrasts than major syllables. Such syllables do not occur on the final edge of a word and may be derived through shortening of syllables in weak prosodic positions; in these iambic languages that is the initial edge of a prosodic foot. [p.222] LTZ is analyzed in terms of an underlying H vs. L vs. toneless distinction on all syllables. 5134.exq_: In LTZ, tone is not predictable from syllable structure, and minor syllables can surface with L, M, or H pitch, as in the following words: tlà sah ‘let boil,’ ra møø ‘bamboo,’ and rá lɨɨ ‘ocean.’
5134.tone: Zophei is a tone language: 'LTZ is analyzed in terms of an underlying H vs. L vs. toneless distinction on all syllables' (p.222); tone is lexical on morphemes ('Underlying H tone morphemes are those which never surface as L; underlying L tone morphemes are those which never surface as H; and underlying toneless morphemes are not limited in their surface pitch', p.222). The only prominence statement is structural: the sesquisyllable is an iamb, weak minor syllable(s) + strong major syllable, minor syllables barred from the final edge (pp.141, 237); the author says it is 'not often clear whether contouring is licensed by the final edge or the prominent syllable' since they coincide (p.247). Unlike Hakha Lai/Lemi, LTZ minor syllables keep an L/M/H pitch contrast and a major syllable shortened to a minor one keeps its tone (bèh + tsih -> bà tsih, p.239). The word 'stress' is never applied to Zophei in the dissertation; the only 'accented on the last' line (p.233, p.215) is Stilson 1866 quoted on Khimi/Mro. The family-level companion paper (Lotven et al. 2020, JSALL 6(2), p.15) says 'In sesquisyllabic words, a stressed "major syllable" is preceded by a short, unstressed C or CV "minor syllable"... resulting in an iambic (unstressed-stressed) word structure' -- a Kuki-Chin generalisation, not a Zophei-specific rule.

5136.prule: Primary stress falls on the first vowel that is preceded by a consonant: the initial syllable in consonant- or cluster-initial words (kápan 'short', ŋgóðRo 'black'), the second syllable in vowel-initial words (ayóŋ 'I', alán 'sky', aðá 'crow'); an onsetless initial vowel is never stressed. The Proto-Trukic reconstruction counts morae ('beginning with the penultimate mora and assigning stress to every second mora to the left'), i.e. a long vowel or vowel sequence carries two stress positions (items with *au split into *a-stressed and *u-stressed sets); the source does not define the mora.
5143.prule: No placement rule is stated for Saipan Carolinian. The only rule in the sources is Jackson's reconstruction for Proto-Trukic (the ancestor): stress on the penultimate mora and on every second mora to its left (right-to-left alternating, mora-counting). 5153.prule: No positional stress rule. Ekajuk is a two-level tone language (H, L, plus automatic downstep D). Stress is called lexical and 'goes normally with the high tones', i.e. it is a correlate of high tone rather than an independent position computable from syllable count or weight. A closed set of morphemes (object-pronoun clitics -m -a -e -r -n, the clitic -a, and the initial vowel of area 'much', eji 'when', ana 'like that', owo 'then') carries inherent stress whatever its tone.

tn.quote: There are two tonal levels in Ekajuk, namely high (H) and low (L) plus a feature of downstep lowering automatically all high tones after low tones within certain grammatical units. After a downstep a new pitch level is established, although the interval between H and L is gradually narrowed. The symbol D is used for an established downstepped high tone. Since tone (like stress) is a feature of the word and all com- binations of L H and D are found, compressions of tones are common in one-syllable words. Compressed tones are written with juxtapposed letterss. HL for downglide, LH for upglide.

5155.prule: No rule is stated in any reachable source: the three SIL items are bare Expanded Philippine Word List field sheets whose only key is '? = glottal'. Nickell writes an acute on one vowel of most entries, on the ultima in some words (abaká, kagát, uták, toláng, isú?, sikə́d, maluwág, natáy, aggáw, masiddúg, ilibúng) and on the penult in others of the same shape (mapúray, sínay, gáta?, dúpa, dígu?, dága?, sámi, útta, lárəm, masíddug), so the marks are not computable from syllable count; but the acute is nowhere defined, the same words are marked on different syllables in the two lists made two days apart in neighbouring villages (77207 masiddúg, gáta?, butalí?, daga?, gatang vs 77200 masíddug, gatə́?, butáli?, dága?, gátang), forms marked in one copy are unmarked in another (dakəl, ngamin, sinay, dulay), and in the only Faire-proper list by another hand (77208 original) every penult acute sits on a colon-marked long vowel (dá:ga, á:tu?, amí:mum, talí:nga?) while uncoloned words take the acute on the ultima (anák, algáw, dabbúm). The sheets are therefore consistent both with lexically placed penult/ultima stress and with fixed ultima stress plus contrastive length, and cannot decide between them.

5158.tone: Author's own label is 'tone-accent language' (citing Hayward 1999 on cumulative prominence): one H per simple word, carried by the syllable nucleus, long vowels take one level tone never a contour (p. 26); H placement distinguishes words (máo 'to dress' vs maó 'cloth', gobá 'be brave' vs góba 'brave', p. 26).
